question: A train's two wheels on one axle are fixed together, so they must spin at exactly the same rate. Yet on a curve the outer rail is longer than the inner one. How does a train get round a bend without one wheel skidding?
correct_answer: Cone-shaped wheels roll on different diameters
alternative_answers: Tapered wheel treads act like a differential
The axle shifts sideways so the outer wheel rolls on a bigger circumference
Wheels are wider at the flange so the outer one uses a larger diameter
headline_answer: Cone-shaped wheels roll on different diameters
source_excerpt: when one wheel is pushed closer to the adjacent (outer) rail, it presents a bigger circumference to the rail than when centred on the track.

extra.verification_notes: Standard explanation: conical wheel treads let the outer wheel roll on a larger diameter than the inner on curves (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_wheel).

explanation: Railway wheels are not flat cylinders but slightly cone-shaped, wider near the inside flange and narrower at the outer edge. On a curve the whole axle slides a little toward the outside of the bend, so the outer wheel rides on its fat part and the inner wheel on its thin part. Spinning at the same rate, the outer wheel now covers more ground per turn than the inner one, exactly what the longer outer rail needs. The axle effectively steers itself, and the flanges only touch the rail as a last resort on very tight curves.

question: The curving stone viaduct that the Hogwarts Express crosses in the Harry Potter films is a real railway bridge. In which country?
source_excerpt: The viaduct is built on a curve of 792 feet (241 m).

extra.why_interesting: The curved viaduct looks like a fantasy set, but it is a working 19th-century railway bridge that tourists can ride a real steam train across today.
extra.verification_notes: Glenfinnan Viaduct, a curved stone railway viaduct in Lochaber, Scotland, appears in the Harry Potter films as the Hogwarts Express route.

explanation: It is the 21-arch Glenfinnan Viaduct on the West Highland Line, and a real steam train still crosses it every summer with fans leaning out of the windows.

question: The longest perfectly straight stretch of railway track in the world runs for 478 kilometres across a flat, treeless plain. On which continent?
source_excerpt: longest straight stretch of railway track in the world... 478.193 kilometres (297.135 miles)

extra.why_interesting: Players assume railways always curve around something; here there is nothing to curve around for nearly 500 km.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the 478 km straight section on the Trans-Australian Railway across the Nullarbor Plain, Australia; no newer record found.

explanation: It crosses the Nullarbor Plain, whose Latin-derived name literally means no trees, and the Indian Pacific train takes several hours to cover the straight without a single bend.

question: In which year did Japan's first bullet train line, from Tokyo to Osaka, carry its first passengers?
source_excerpt: The Tokaido Shinkansen opened on October 1, 1964, connecting Tokyo to Shin-Ōsaka, in time for the 1964 Summer Olympics.

extra.why_interesting: Most players place high-speed rail in the 1980s or later; Japan was running 210 km/h bullet trains while the Beatles were still together.
extra.verification_notes: Tokaido Shinkansen (Tokyo–Osaka) opened on October 1, 1964, which matches the claimed answer; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokaido_Shinkansen

explanation: The line opened just nine days before Tokyo hosted the Summer Olympics, showing the world a Japan rebuilt and racing ahead at 210 km/h.

question: In 1869 a golden spike was hammered in to join the two halves of America's first coast-to-coast railroad. In which US state did the rails meet?
source_excerpt: Promontory Summit marks the site where the First Transcontinental Railroad was completed May 10, 1869, from Omaha to Sacramento

extra.why_interesting: Players expect the coast-to-coast line to have been joined somewhere dramatic like California or the Rockies, not in a remote Utah desert.
extra.verification_notes: The golden spike joined the Union Pacific and Central Pacific at Promontory Summit, which is now in Utah (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promontory_Summit); Utah was a territory in 1869, which is a negligible nuance.

explanation: The ceremony took place at Promontory Summit near the Great Salt Lake, and the journey from New York to San Francisco shrank from months to about a week.

question: The longest railway tunnel in the world opened in 2016 and runs for 57 kilometres beneath a mountain range. Which country built it?
source_excerpt: Gotthard Base Tunnel in Switzerland remains the world's longest conventional railway tunnel at 57,104 m, opened in 2016.

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for the Channel Tunnel or something in Japan; the record holder is a flat route bored straight through the Alps.
extra.verification_notes: Gotthard Base Tunnel (Switzerland, opened 2016, ~57 km) remains the world's longest railway tunnel per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_longest_tunnels.

explanation: The Gotthard Base Tunnel lets trains cross the Alps on an almost flat track, and it beat Japan's Seikan Tunnel to the record by several kilometres.

question: Until 2018, every long-distance train timetable across Russia, even in Vladivostok seven hours ahead, showed times according to the clock of which single city?
source_excerpt: Russia announced it would stop running all long-distance trains across its 11 time zones on Moscow time, ending a frequent cause of confusion for travellers.

extra.why_interesting: The Trans-Siberian crosses seven time zones, yet for over a century a passenger in Vladivostok reading a departure board was looking at a clock set thousands of kilometres away.
extra.verification_notes: Russian long-distance trains ran on Moscow time until Aug 2018, when local time replaced it; Vladivostok is +7h from Moscow (https://www.france24.com/en/20180725-russian-trains-end-dependence-moscow-time).

explanation: Russian Railways ran its whole network on Moscow time, so a Trans-Siberian passenger might board at what the timetable called four in the morning while the sun was high overhead.

question: The railway to Lhasa in Tibet climbs above 5,000 metres. What do its carriages pump in for passengers that no other ordinary train needs to?
source_excerpt: each seat in the train is equipped with an oxygen supply outlet for any possible emergency.

extra.why_interesting: Players think of a train as the gentle way to travel; here the route is so high that the carriages need equipment normally associated with hospitals or aircraft.
extra.verification_notes: Qinghai–Tibet Railway reaches 5,072 m and its carriages have oxygen enrichment and per-seat oxygen outlets; no newer development found that overturns this.

explanation: The line crests the Tanggula Pass at 5,072 metres, where the air is so thin that the sealed carriages are enriched with oxygen and have outlets by the seats.

question: Which city's famous railway terminal, with 44 platforms stacked on two underground levels, has more platforms than any other station in the world?
source_excerpt: Grand Central covers 48 acres (19 ha) and has 44 platforms, more than any other railroad station in the world.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect the record in a rail-mad country like Japan, Germany or China; the answer is a commuter terminal in a city most associate with the subway.
extra.verification_notes: Grand Central Terminal in New York has 44 platforms on two underground levels, the most of any station; no newer record found (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Terminal).

explanation: Grand Central Terminal hides its platforms beneath the celebrated main concourse, and all of them are dead ends serving commuter trains rather than long-distance routes.

question: Named after a water bird, which British steam locomotive set the world speed record for steam at 203 km/h in 1938, a record never beaten?

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a 1930s record would have fallen long ago; steam was abandoned before anyone bothered to beat it, so a duck-named engine remains champion.
extra.verification_notes: Mallard's 126 mph (203 km/h) on 3 July 1938 remains the officially recognised steam speed record; no newer record found per Wikipedia.

explanation: Mallard hit the mark on a downhill stretch near Grantham, and since steam engines vanished from mainlines in the following decades, nobody ever came back to challenge it.

question: Australia's north-to-south transcontinental train, from Adelaide to Darwin, takes its name from camel drivers who came to the outback from which country?
source_excerpt: The name derives from 'The Afghan Express'... honors Afghan camel drivers who arrived in Australia in the late 19th century.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect an Australian train to be named after a river, an explorer or an animal; instead it honours camel drivers from Central Asia.
extra.verification_notes: The Ghan is named for 'Afghan' camel drivers, and Afghanistan is the standard answer, though Wikipedia notes the drivers also came from India, which is a minor nuance.

explanation: The train is called The Ghan, short for Afghan, and the cameleers it honours hauled supplies across the desert along roughly the route the rails now follow.

question: In Agatha Christie's most famous railway mystery, a snowdrift traps the Orient Express and its passengers overnight. In which country, as it was then called, does the train come to a halt?
source_excerpt: caught far beyond Vinkovci station in Yugoslavia (today Croatia)

extra.why_interesting: Everyone knows the train gets stuck in snow, but almost nobody thinks about where; the glamorous express is stranded in the Balkans, not the Alps.
extra.verification_notes: The novel places the snowbound train in Yugoslavia, beyond Vinkovci (now Croatia), so the answer is correct as the country was then called.

explanation: Christie strands the train between Vinkovci and Brod in what is now Croatia, giving Hercule Poirot a sealed carriage full of suspects and nowhere for the killer to run.

question: Australia's famous Ghan train crosses the continent from Adelaide to Darwin. Its name honours which group of people who travelled that route long before the rails did?
source_excerpt: may honor Afghan camel drivers who arrived in Australia in the late 19th century to help the British colonists find a way to reach the country's interior.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect an Australian outback train to be named after an explorer, a town or an animal; the answer reveals that camels and the men who drove them from Afghanistan and the Indian subcontinent were the original transport of the interior.
extra.verification_notes: The Ghan's name derives from 'The Afghan Express', commonly said to honour the Afghan camel drivers; the route is still Adelaide–Darwin (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ghan).

explanation: Camel trains led by cameleers known collectively as Afghans supplied the outback in the nineteenth century, and the railway that replaced them was nicknamed the Afghan Express, soon shortened to the Ghan.
